evidence.title: Consistency of a clinical decision support system with molecular tumour board recommendations for tumour sequencing-guided treatment of pancreatic cancer
evidence.outcome: Whether expert molecular tumour board review of CDSS genomic actionability outputs supports their validity
evidence.effect: MTB endorsed molecularly informed options in 21 cases but excluded no drugs based on inefficacy or toxicity markers; evidence for actionability was weak; 8 patients got targeted treatment without benefit.
evidence.quote: The overall evidence underpinning assertions of actionability was weak.

evidence.title: PhysiCase: Development and dual-layer validation of synthetic cases for health professional education: A pilot study leveraging Generative AI
evidence.outcome: expert detection of clinical reasoning failures in synthetic cases
evidence.effect: Automated screening passed 70.3% of cases, but expert review identified subtle clinical reasoning failures; medical accuracy CVI was 87.5%, with GPT-4.1 achieving 4.10/5 accuracy and Llama 4 Scout showing the lowest ratings.
evidence.quote: The dual-layer validation framework proved methodologically viable: automated screening efficiently reduced expert review burden, while human judgment remained indispensable for detecting subtle clinical reasoning failures.

evidence.title: Improving the readability of trauma patient education materials: a ChatGPT solution demonstrated using materials by the Orthopaedic Trauma Association
evidence.venue: OTA international : the open access journal of orthopaedic trauma
evidence.outcome: Expert surgeon review identifying content omissions in ChatGPT-revised patient education articles
evidence.effect: Expert review flagged 12 of 41 (29.3%) revised articles needing edits for omissions, oversimplification or loss of accuracy; 16 (39%) titles needed revision.
evidence.quote: However, nearly a third (29.3%) of the ChatGPT revised articles required revisions due to content omissions, thus highlighting the importance of expert review.

evidence.title: Can a Generative Artificial Intelligence Model Be Used to Create Mass Casualty Incident Simulation Scenarios? A Feasibility Study
evidence.effect: Median SSET score improved from 78.5 (IQR 74-82) pre-revision to 94 (IQR 93-96) post-revision.
evidence.quote: Following secondary human revision and iterative refinement, the LLM-generated scenarios improved, achieving a median SSET score of 94 (IQR 93-96) with an interrater reliability ICC of 0.7425.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM-generated mass casualty simulation scenarios (62 simulated patients), plus 2 public control scenarios

evidence.title: Evaluating large language models for simplifying non-English medical consent with clinician involvement
evidence.effect: Risk score 3.28 to 3.69, p = 0.016; overall 2.86 to 3.64, p = 0.004.
evidence.quote: The risk score increased from 3.28 (SD = 0.55) to 3.69 (SD = 0.66), p = 0.016; the overall score also rose from 2.86 (SD = 0.36) to 3.64 (SD = 0.31), p = 0.004.

evidence.title: Using large language models to enhance clinically-driven missing data recovery algorithms in electronic health records
evidence.effect: Clinicians endorsed 421 of 514 (82%) LLM-context ICD-10 code matches.
evidence.quote: Of the 514 ICD-10 codes matching patients in our sample based on LLMs (context), at least 1 clinician endorsed 421 of them ( 82 % ).

evidence.title: Human-in-the-loop validation of a sequential multi-LLM medical education pipeline
evidence.outcome: error identification by attending radiologists versus residents
evidence.effect: attending radiologists identified more errors than residents (OR 4.52, 95% CI 2.38-8.57), though workload-matched sensitivity analyses attenuated this gap
evidence.quote: In unadjusted analyses, attending radiologists identified more errors than residents (odds ratio 4.52, 95% CI 2.38-8.57), although workload-matched sensitivity analyses attenuated this gap.

evidence.title: Large language models versus expert clinicians in optimizing Chinese patient education materials for temporomandibular disorders: a mixed-methods study integrating readability, accuracy, actionability, and cultural adaptability
evidence.outcome: Whether expert review corrects domain-specific errors in LLM-generated TCM and procedural content
evidence.effect: Expert-revised LLM texts improved accuracy from 3.23 to 4.49; TCM topics remained lowest across groups (Group C 3.8; Group D 4.0), and LLM TCM depth was limited.
evidence.quote: Critically, the human-AI collaboration model remediated these accuracy deficits, achieving accuracy equivalent to clinician-only texts.

evidence.venue: Studies in health technology and informatics
evidence.outcome: Share of ChatGPT-generated term definitions that experts needed to correct

evidence.title: Benchmarking generative AI tools for literature retrieval and summarization in genomic variant interpretation
evidence.outcome: Reliability of AI-generated genomic variant literature summaries as judged by blinded domain experts
evidence.effect: Tool performance varied widely and was sensitive to literature scarcity; authors conclude reliable integration requires expert validation and domain-related fine-tuning.
evidence.quote: While some platforms already provide useful outputs, reliable integration into basic and clinical research requires expert validation and domain-related fine-tuning.

evidence.title: Clinical decision support in hematological malignancies using a case-grounded AI agent
evidence.outcome: Automated somatic variant classification errors against expert reference classifications
evidence.effect: Classification agreed with the reference for 56/70 variants; sensitivity was 0.88 and specificity 0.84. No expert likely oncogenic/oncogenic variant was classified as likely benign/benign.
evidence.quote: Using three clinically pragmatic bins (likely benign/benign (LB/B), variant of uncertain significance (VUS), likely oncogenic/oncogenic (LO/O)), HemaGuide concurred with the reference for 56/70 variants (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Table 6 ).

evidence.title: Real-world evaluation of deep learning algorithms to classify functional pathogenic germline variants
evidence.effect: For variants of uncertain significance, models were generally of limited clinical utility.
evidence.quote: However, when specifically tasked with classifying variants of uncertain significance, the deep learning models were generally of limited clinical utility.

evidence.title: Dosimetric comparison of autocontouring techniques for online adaptive proton therapy
evidence.outcome: dosimetric effect of automatic target contour
evidence.effect: >5% prescribed dose in most cases; manual verification remains necessary
evidence.quote: Contrarily, the dosimetric effect of using the automatic target contour was larger (>5% prescribed dose in most cases), indicating that manual verification of that contour remains necessary.

commentary.bottom_line: In two offline studies, experts corrected 28.99% of AI-generated term definitions and flagged 12 of 41 (29.3%) revised articles for edits, but eight of the nine tests were offline and mostly concerned educational content, and the one real genomic deployment (39 patients) gave mixed results. No study compared errors reaching patients with and without expert review.

perspectives.view: Nine studies test expert review, but eight are offline evaluations without a comparison group. Most concern patient education or training material rather than specialized outputs such as variant calls. The single real deployment, a molecular tumour board reviewing genomic outputs for 39 patients, returned mixed findings. No study measured errors reaching patients, so certainty is very low.

Automated somatic variant classification agreed with the expert reference for 56 of 70 variants, and automatic contours shifted dose by more than 5% in most cases. Experts found reasoning failures in synthetic cases that automated screening had passed. One tumour board excluded no drugs, and 8 patients received targeted therapy without benefit, which suggests review may miss weak actionability evidence.

Reviewer seniority appears to matter. Attending radiologists identified more errors than residents (OR 4.52, 95% CI 2.38-8.57), though the gap narrowed when workload was matched. Clinicians endorsed 421 of 514 (82%) LLM-suggested ICD-10 matches, which suggests review often confirms output rather than correcting it. No study reported reviewer time or how review fit into daily workflow.

Three studies included non-English speakers and one included low health literacy readers, all in China or Spain and all on consent or education text. Clinician review raised consent risk scores from 3.28 to 3.69, and expert revision raised accuracy from 3.23 to 4.49. Traditional Chinese medicine topics scored lowest in every group, which the authors linked to limited LLM depth.

Experts corrected 28.99% of ChatGPT term definitions and flagged 12 of 41 (29.3%) revised articles for edits, so in these two studies about three in ten outputs returned to a specialist. None of the studies measured reviewer hours, cost, or turnaround time, and staffing needs for genomic review therefore remain unestimated.

In the consent study, four laypersons joined four surgeons as raters, and overall quality scores rose from 2.86 to 3.64 after clinician review (p = 0.004). No study asked patients whether expert sign-off affected their trust or whether they could reach the reviewing specialist.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares genomic or other specialized AI outputs with and without expert review in live care and counts the errors that reach patients. Prospective studies should also record reviewer time, reviewer qualifications, and results in safety-net laboratories and clinics.
commentary.underserved_note: Three tests included limited English proficiency or non-English populations and one included low health literacy readers, but all were offline studies of educational or consent text in China and Spain. No test included U.S. Medicaid or safety-net settings, so the evidence says little about expert review of genomic outputs for those patients, where specialist access may be more limited.
